executive_assessment.text: Comparative district flood/drought and heat indices identify named differences; outdoor workers, people with limited shelter and other vulnerable groups face different coping constraints.

A national study finds drought–IPV associations, with different samples for precipitation and socioeconomic drought, but cannot establish causality or income mediation. Heat-plan counts describe planning coverage, not effectiveness.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2024-12-17 reports: The district assessment placed 51 districts in very high and 118 in high flood-risk bands; about 85% of those districts are in Assam, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat, Odisha and Jammu and Kashmir.

Source dated 2024-12-17 reports: The assessment placed 91 districts in very high and 188 in high drought-risk bands; more than 85% of these districts are in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Chhattisgarh, Kerala, Uttarakhand and Haryana.

Source dated 2024-12-17 reports: Among the 50 districts with highest flood risk and 50 with highest drought risk, 11 were very high risk for both, including Patna, Alappuzha, Charaideo, Dibrugarh, Sibsagar, South Salmara-Mankachar, Golaghat, Kendrapara, Murshidabad, Nadia and Uttar Dinajpur.

Source dated 2025-05-20 reports: CEEW classed 417 of 734 districts (57%), home to 76% of residents, at high or very high heat risk; Delhi, Maharashtra, Goa, Kerala and Gujarat ranked among the highest-risk states.

Source dated 2025-05-20 reports: Comparing 2012–2022 with 1982–2011, CEEW found extra warm nights per summer in Mumbai (15), Bengaluru (11), Bhopal and Jaipur (7 each), Delhi (6) and Chennai (4); warm nights rose faster than hot days.

Source dated 2025-05-20 reports: CEEW found high heat vulnerability in districts of seven named states, where heat combined with chronic illness, older people and under-fives; Odisha districts with green cover and blue infrastructure had lower vulnerability.

Source dated 2026-07-20 reports: Delhi's SAPCC 2.0 assessment identifies South Delhi as most and New Delhi as least climate-vulnerable; it projects higher summer maximum temperatures and more very hot days by mid-century, with cool roofs, cooling corridors, green infrastructure, drainage and wetland measures envisaged.

Source dated 2025-05-01 reports: NHRC cited 3,798 NCRB-recorded heat and sun-stroke deaths in 2018–2022 and identified economically weaker people, outdoor workers, older people, children and homeless people as at risk from inadequate shelter and resources; it urged 11 states to provide protections.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 10 of 10 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.

A peer-reviewed national study provides explicit drought–intimate-partner-violence associations but cannot establish causality or test the proposed household-income pathway; this is not evidence of an armed-conflict pathway.
The reviewed material does not directly establish that conflict or insecurity changes climate exposure or blocks adaptation access.
District heat classifications use 1982–2022 hazard data with older Census and NFHS indicators; they should not be read as a refreshed 2026 risk inventory.
No complete causal income-mediated drought→IPV chain is assembled: the study explicitly could not test the proposed mediator. The two drought definitions have different analytical samples.
District hazard/risk examples are not assigned the national study's violence associations as local effect estimates. No armed-conflict pathway or reverse insecurity constraint was verified.
Draft extension: human source review and approval remain pending. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
